newsitem.title: MEXICO: Albright, Mexico play down drug differences.
newsitem.headline: Albright, Mexico play down drug differences.

text.p: The United States and Mexico on Monday sought to play down differences over the fight against drug trafficking that have threatened to cloud President Bill Clinton's first state visit here this week.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright acknowledged at a news conference here that bilateral relations were "as broad and deep and as complex as any two nations have."
However, drugs, she said, "have to be dealt with cooperatively."
In a speech to Cabinet members from both countries in Mexico City, her Mexican counterpart, Jose Angel Gurria, called for an end to cross-border friction over drugs.

"It would be a tragedy for both our countries that drug traffickers would benefit while our governments are involved in a sterile and irritating exercise of allocating blame," he told the Mexico-U.S. Binational Commission.
The concept of cooperation cropped up frequently during a joint news conference prior to the bilateral commission meeting, and Albright avoided treading on local sensibilities.

Prior to Clinton's trip, the Mexican government reacted angrily to suggestions in Washington that U.S. drug agents bear arms in Mexico. Violence by drug gangs has increased in the country through which most cocaine flows into the United States.

Mexico has also criticised the White House's policy of "certifying", or publicly judging, the anti-drug efforts of countries around the world -- particularly poignant in Mexico this year because its performance received criticism.
Albright applauded Mexico's measures to crack down on drugs and praised President Ernesto Zedillo as a "determined partner" in the anti-narcotics battle.

Repeatedly questioned by Mexican journalists about whether the U.S. government would press for the arming of Drug Enforcement Administration agents in Mexico, she lumped the dangers to Mexican and U.S. agents together.
"We, therefore, must work together to guarantee their safety," she said.
Gurria echoed Zedillo's promise that no U.S. agent would bear arms in Mexico.
Albright said the two countries had taken "many forward steps" to halt the flow of drugs through Mexico to consumers in the United States.

"But we know that in the struggle between law and outlaw, between democratic integrity and corrupt expediency we are neither winning nor losing, but remain in the hottest stages of battle," Albright told the Binational Commission.

She praised steps to stamp out money laundering and ease extradition of traffickers. But, she said, "we must follow up on last year's high narcotics seizure rates by intensifying joint operations and putting major traffickers behind bars."

Underscoring the continued doubts in Washington about Mexican drug policy, U.S. Senator Phil Gramm on Monday urged Clinton to raise in Mexico the case of convicted drug trafficker Rafael Caro Quintero, who last month won an appeal in a Mexican court against his sentence for the 1985 killing of DEA agent Enrique Camarena.

He said the decision, "coming amid the mounting evidence of drug corruption in Mexico, is not reassuring to anyone concerned about justice for Agent Camerena's killers or about the river of drugs and death that continues to flow from Mexico into Texas."
